Art teacher's note: fest banner, Thursday

At 2:30 today the principal asked for a welcome banner for tomorrow's fest, and the art room only had until 4:00. I asked Lalremsiami, from Class 10, to lead it. She didn't start painting at once, and she didn't spend an hour planning either. She said out loud, "No time for a perfect design. Three quick ideas, ten minutes, then pick." She sketched three small layouts in pencil: one with the school crest in the middle, one with big letters across, one with a border of flowers. Pallavi and two others voted for the big letters, since they could be read from the gate. By 3:55 the banner was drying. It was not fancy, but it was clear and bright.

qa.a: Ten minutes, for three quick ideas.

qa.a: Pallavi likely felt included and practical, choosing the big letters because they could be read from the gate.

Friday

At lunch the fest coordinator grabbed me: "Tejas, we need a banner for the quiz stage. By six." It was already two. My first instinct was to plan it properly, like my geography project: grid, colours, measurements. Then I thought, "That took me a week. I have four hours, and I've never made a banner. If I plan properly, I'll still be planning at six." So I did it the rough way. Three tiny sketches on the back of my notebook, five minutes each. One with a question mark, one with a lightbulb, one with just big letters. Imran picked the lightbulb. We painted it on old chart paper. It was up by 5:40. Honestly? It looked good. Rough and quick was the right call.

subtype: Approach: acts quickly when time is short and the situation is urgent [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Payal,

I hope you're feeling better today. I wanted to write down what happened last night, because you said you don't remember much.

We were at the hostel cultural night, clapping for the dance group, when you suddenly went pale and slid off your chair. For a second everyone froze. I didn't think about what to do, there was no time to plan. I shouted, "Someone get the warden!" and knelt by you so you wouldn't be alone. I asked the girls to step back and give you air, and a senior from the first-aid club came over. The warden called the campus doctor, who came within minutes and took over. Your parents have been told.

Please rest. I'll bring you dinner tonight.

Yamini

qa.a: They were at the hostel cultural night, clapping for the dance group.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when Payal slid off the chair?
qa.a: Yamini felt a jolt of fear, and everyone froze for a second, but there was no time to plan, so Yamini acted at once.

qa.q: Why was acting quickly right here, instead of planning?
qa.a: It was urgent, so the useful steps were simple: call the warden, stay close and give air until the doctor took over.

qa.q: How might Payal feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Payal would likely feel grateful and cared for, learning how quickly a friend acted and stayed close the whole time.

subtype: Approach: acts quickly when time is short and the situation is urgent [Thinking]
passage: I'm Ishita, and people ask me what I did the night Maria fainted, like I had a plan. I didn't. I caught her arm so her head didn't hit the floor. My brain just went: help, now. I shouted for the warden and told the boy nearest the door to run to the security desk. I sat with Maria on the floor and kept talking to her. The warden came in two minutes, called the campus doctor, and cleared a space. There was no time to think about the best way. The best way was the fastest.

subtype: Approach: takes time and sleeps on it when the decision is slow and important [Thinking]
passage: Nirmala had a month before she needed to tell the college whether she'd join the master's programme or take the job offer. Her family's phone line was bad that month, and her parents in the village could only talk on Sunday evenings. Her friend Sarita said, "Just decide tonight, what's the big deal?" Nirmala shook her head. "This is two years of my life. No one is rushing me. Why should I rush myself?" So she took the month. She asked two seniors about the master's, read about the job's training programme, and wrote the facts on two pages. Each Sunday she called home, and her parents asked questions she hadn't thought of. By the last week, she slept on it twice. Then she chose the job, feeling calm.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when she finally chose the job?

qa.a: It was important and slow, with no deadline forcing speed, so gathering facts and family views made a better choice.

qa.q: How does Sarita see Nirmala's slowness?

In the fourth week he stopped adding and just looked, and slept on it. In the fifth, he chose to work first and defer. He felt settled.

subtype: Approach: plans alone for a personal decision [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: Karthik's semester timetable was out, and everyone in the hostel had advice. His friend Anand said, "Study in the library from six to ten, like us." Karthik thought, "I know I can't focus in the library. I work best early, and I'm useless after nine."

Wednesday: He sat alone on his bed with a notebook and planned: five to seven in the morning for hard subjects, lectures, a nap after lunch, lighter reading from four to six, and nothing after nine. He didn't ask anyone. "Nobody else knows my habits. This is mine to decide."

Two Mondays later: He'd kept it every day. His lab reports were on time. Anand shrugged. "Weird schedule. But it works for you."

qa.q: Why did planning alone suit this decision?
qa.a: It was personal and depended on his own habits, so others' advice, like the library, would add little.

qa.a: Anand finds it weird but accepts that it works for him.

grounding: A student chooses his own study schedule alone, since he knows his own habits and others' input would add little.

subtype: Approach: plans alone for a personal decision [Thinking]
passage: Ritu, you're asking everyone how to plan your study time. Let me tell you what your Vaibhav Mama did. In college, I asked five friends for their schedules. One studied at night, one in the library, one with music. I tried each for a week. None worked, because none of them was me. Then one Sunday I sat alone on the roof with a notebook and thought honestly: when am I sharp? Mornings. When am I lazy? After lunch. Where can I focus? Only at my own desk. I wrote my timetable in half an hour, without asking anybody. It lasted all four years. For some things, beta, you need other people. For your own habits, you're the expert.

qa.a: Sitting alone to think honestly about his own habits; he knew himself better than any friend could.

qa.q: How might the five friends have felt about Vaibhav not using their schedules?

subtype: Approach: plans as a group when several people share the result [Thinking]
passage: I'm Pranav, and I live on the third floor of the hostel. Our floor had fights about everything: music at night, the fridge, bathroom cleaning. Gautam, our floor rep, could have just written rules and pinned them up. Instead, one evening, he knocked on all twelve doors and said, "Common room, eight o'clock, everyone." I asked him later why he didn't just decide. He said, "If I make the rules alone, nobody will follow them. Everyone uses the floor, so everyone has to agree." At the meeting people argued, laughed and voted. Quiet hours after eleven. Fridge cleaned Sundays. A cleaning rota by room. It took ninety minutes. Six weeks later, the rules on the notice board are still being followed.

qa.q: How many doors did Gautam knock on?
qa.a: All twelve doors.

qa.q: What was Gautam thinking when he called a meeting instead of deciding alone?

qa.q: Why did a group meeting suit this problem?
qa.a: Everyone shares the floor, so rules everyone helped make are more likely to be accepted and followed.

qa.q: How might the other residents see the meeting?
qa.a: They likely felt heard and more willing to follow rules they had voted on.

grounding: A hostel floor deciding on shared rules holds a meeting, since rules made by one person would not be accepted by the rest.

subtype: Approach: uses one method for every problem out of habit [Pitfall]
passage: Abhinav, you're stuck on your short film script? Let me tell your Thomas Uncle's story. In college, I was the timetable king. Every exam, every assignment, planned to the half hour, and it worked beautifully for engineering. Then I joined the drama club and had to write a one-act play. What did I do? A timetable. "Monday 6 to 7: Scene 1. Tuesday 6 to 7: Scene 2." Monday at six I sat down, and nothing came. At seven I had two lines and felt like a failure. Tuesday, the same. For two weeks I kept the timetable and wrote almost nothing. Creative work doesn't come on schedule. My friend finally said, "Just scribble anything, anywhere." I'd never tried that. I'd used one method for everything.

qa.a: After the first blocked evening; trying a loose start, like scribbling ideas anywhere, would have suited the play better.

qa.q: How might Thomas's friend have felt watching him struggle?
qa.a: The friend probably felt concerned and a little impatient, which is why they suggested scribbling anything.

grounding: An elder recalls using detailed timetables even for creative writing, where a loose start would have suited better, and feeling blocked.

subtype: Approach: matches effort to reversibility, deciding fast on reversible choices and slow on one-way ones [Thinking]
passage:
"Kishore, you picked that phone plan in two minutes?"
"Yeah. It's monthly. If it's bad, I switch next month. Why waste an evening?"
"But you've been looking at flats for three weeks."
"Vikas, that's different. The flat is an eleven-month agreement. If I hate it, I can't just leave. I'd lose the deposit and have to find another place."
"So fast for the phone, slow for the flat."
"Exactly. Fast when I can undo it. Slow when I can't."
"What have you checked so far?"
"Water supply in summer, the landlord's rules on guests, the walk to the metro at night, the lock-in clause." Kishore tapped his notebook. "I'm seeing the last one on Saturday with my cousin."
"And the phone?"
"Already using it. It's fine."

qa.q: How long is the flat agreement?
qa.a: Eleven months.

qa.q: What does Kishore's careful checking of the flat suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels cautious and a bit anxious about being stuck, because the flat can't easily be undone.

qa.q: Why is Kishore's approach sensible?
qa.a: He puts little effort into choices he can reverse, like the monthly plan, and much more into one-way choices like a long agreement.

qa.q: How does Vikas see Kishore's different speeds at first?
qa.a: Vikas is puzzled at first, then understands the reasoning.

grounding: A student picks a phone plan quickly because he can change it, but takes weeks over a rental agreement that is hard to leave.

subtype: Approach: matches effort to reversibility, deciding fast on reversible choices and slow on one-way ones [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: uses brainstorming for a novel problem with no known answer [Thinking]
passage: In the meeting room of the telemedicine start-up, Zubin put one question on the screen: "Elderly patients in small towns miss video appointments. Why, and what can we do?" We need lots of ideas first, then pick." For twenty-five minutes, everyone threw ideas on sticky notes: phone-call option, a helper at the local pharmacy, reminder calls in the local language, larger buttons, appointments at the village health centre. subtype: Approach: uses precedent for a familiar problem [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: uses precedent for a familiar problem [Thinking]
passage: At the community library in Vancouver, Wei had coordinated the spring reading workshop for children for four years. grounding: An experienced coordinator plans a routine workshop by reusing last year's plan and changing only dates and venue.
